title: The Template That Knew Its Parent
premise:
A web page is two files: a layout with holes in it, and a member list that fills the holes. Jinja's job is to turn that pair of strings into one correct, injection-safe HTML document 
i

 and to do it fast enough to be worth caching. The story follows one string, the source of `members.html`, from the moment a DictLoader hands it over, through lexing, parsing, code generation and `exec`, until it comes back as rendered HTML with an ampersand safely escaped. Along the way it passes every decision an owner has to vouch for: what gets cached and when it goes stale, when the autoescape question is actually asked, what the generated Python is allowed to do, and who decides which file a template may pull in.

chapters.title: The World It Enters
chapters.data_out: a configured Environment: loader=DictLoader, cache=LRUCache(400), extensions={}, is_async=False, autoescape=<function select_autoescape.<locals>.autoescape>
inputs: the two template sources in scenario.py
facts: `autoescape` arrives as a callable, not a bool; the constructor's own default is `False` (environment.py:313), so escaping is opt-in and here it is opted into by name pattern.
`cache_size=400` becomes an `LRUCache(400)`; `0` disables template caching entirely and a negative size gives an unbounded dict (environment.py:83-93).
`auto_reload` defaults to `True`, so a cached template will be re-checked against its uptodate function before reuse.
`bytecode_cache` is None, so every template miss costs a full parse and compile in-process.

`_environment_config_check` uses `assert` for its invariants (undefined must subclass Undefined, delimiters must differ) 
u2014 those checks disappear under `python -O`.
`load_extensions(env, ())` returns `{}`: in this run no extension can preprocess the source or rewrite the token stream.

open_questions.question: The autoescape callable has been stored but never called. Who asks it whether 'members.html' should be escaped, and when?

chapters.title: Asked For By Name
chapters.data_out: the raw source `'{% extends "base.html" %}\n{% block t\u2026'`, filename None, and an uptodate lambda, handed to Environment.compile
facts:
`parent is None`, so `join_path` is skipped and the caller's name goes straight to the loader 
u2014 the name is the whole authorisation check.
The cache key is `(weakref.ref(self.loader), name)`: two loaders cannot collide, and entries die with their loader.
`make_globals` returns `ChainMap({}, env.globals)`, so per-template globals can never mutate the environment's globals.
`BaseLoader.load` calls `get_source` first and only then considers the bytecode cache; with no bytecode cache the source is compiled every time it is loaded.
`DictLoader.get_source` returns `filename=None`; tracebacks for this template will say `<template>` rather than a path.

DictLoader does no path sanitisation at all 
u2014 it is a dict lookup. The loaders that touch a filesystem (`FileSystemLoader`, `PackageLoader`) route names through `split_template_path`, which rejects `..` segments.

open_questions.question: Nothing is cached yet. What makes a second `get_template('members.html')` cheap, and can the cache hand back a template whose source has since changed?

chapters.title: Cut Into Tokens
chapters.data_in: source string + name='members.html' into Environment.compile \u2192 _parse \u2192 Parser.__init__
chapters.data_out: a TokenStream positioned at Token(lineno=1, type='block_begin', value='{%')
facts: `Environment.compile` wraps the whole pipeline in `except TemplateSyntaxError: self.handle_exception(...)`, which re-raises through `debug.rewrite_traceback_stack` so the error points at a template line, not at compiler internals.
`preprocess` folds the source through every extension in priority order; with no extensions it returns the string unchanged.

`get_lexer` caches Lexer objects in a module-global `LRUCache(50)` keyed by the twelve syntax options 
u2014 lexers are shared across environments that happen to use the same delimiters.
The lexer only classifies characters: unbalanced braces or a stray character raise `TemplateSyntaxError`; no template expression is evaluated here.
Newlines are normalised (`\r\n|\r|\n` \u2192 the configured sequence) and, because `keep_trailing_newline` is False, a single trailing newline is dropped before tokenising.

open_questions.question: Does any part of this template's text get executed while it is being read, or is reading strictly inert?

chapters.title: A Shape Instead Of A String
chapters.data_out: Template(body=[Extends(template=Const('base.html')), Output([TemplateData('\n')]), Block(name='title',\u2026), Output([TemplateData('\n')]), Block(name='content',\u2026)]) with the environment attached to every node
facts:
`subparse` recognises exactly three token kinds 
u2014 data, `{{ \u2026 }}`, `{% \u2026 %}` 
u2014 and `parse_statement` dispatches on a frozen keyword set plus extension-registered tags; anything else goes to `fail_unknown_tag` with a nesting hint.
Every statement must be closed by `expect('block_end')`; a mismatch raises `TemplateSyntaxError` carrying lineno, template name and filename.

Literal text becomes `TemplateData` inside an `Output` node 
u2014 including the lone `'\n'` that sits between `{% extends %}` and `{% block title %}`.
`parse_block` rejects hyphenated block names with a targeted error message and enforces that `required` blocks contain only whitespace or comments.
`set_environment` walks the whole tree and attaches the environment to each node; that is what later lets `as_const()` call real filters during constant folding.

open_questions.question: The extends target folded into a constant string. What would change if a template wrote `{% extends some_variable %}`?
Two `Output(TemplateData('\n'))` nodes now sit at the top level of a template that extends another. Do they get printed?

chapters.title: The Question Is Asked: Code For The Root
chapters.data_in: the Template AST + environment + name='members.html' into generate()
chapters.data_out: generated source so far: imports, `name = 'members.html'`, `def root(context, \u2026)` whose body sets `parent_template = None`, runs the extends, and ends with `yield from parent_template.root_render_func(context)`
facts:
`visit_Template` constructs `EvalContext(environment, 'members.html')`, and `EvalContext.__init__` calls the autoescape callable with the template name 
u2014 this is the first time the question is asked, and the answer is frozen into the emitted code.
`node.find(Extends)` is not None, so `have_extends` is set: the root function declares `parent_template = None` and output statements become conditional.
All `Block` nodes are collected up front; a repeated block name fails compilation with `TemplateAssertionError('block \u2026 defined twice')`.

`visit_Extends` runs at rootlevel, so `has_known_extends` becomes True and `visit_Output` returns immediately for the remaining top-level nodes 
u2014 the stray `'\n'` text is discarded at compile time, never emitted.
A second `{% extends %}` would emit `raise TemplateRuntimeError("extended multiple times")`, or abort the rest of the top-level body via `CompilerExit` when the first extends was already known.
The root function's last act is `yield from parent_template.root_render_func(context)`: a child template never renders its own body directly.

open_questions.question: The root function only defers to the parent. Where does this template's actual HTML end up living?

answers.answer: At compile time: `CodeGenerator.visit_Template` builds an `EvalContext` for the template name, which invokes the autoescape callable and bakes the result into the generated code.
No. Because the extends is at root level, `has_known_extends` is True and `visit_Output` returns before writing anything for top-level text in a child template.

chapters.title: Two Functions Named After Holes, Then Made Real
chapters.data_in: the collected blocks {'title': Block(\u2026), 'content': Block(\u2026)} and the shared EvalContext
facts: Each block becomes a module-level `def block_<name>(context, missing=missing, environment=environment)` with a Frame that is deliberately *not* a child of the root frame, to keep identifier tracking from leaking between them.
Block frames set `block_frame = True` and emit `_block_vars = {}`, so `{% set %}` inside a block does not mutate `context.vars`.
`self` and `super` are only wired into a block when `find_undeclared` spots them in that block's body; here neither appears, so neither is created.

`pull_dependencies` emits a `try/except KeyError` wrapper per filter and test so an unknown name fails as a `TemplateRuntimeError` when called, not when the module loads; this template uses none, so nothing was emitted.
Because the compile-time eval context says autoescape and is not volatile, `visit_Output` escapes constant text at compile time and wraps runtime expressions in `escape(...)` in the generated source.
`debug_info = '1=12&2=17&3=27&5=37&6=41'` maps template line numbers to generated line numbers; it is the mechanism behind template-accurate tracebacks.

`_compile` is the builtin `compile(source, '<template>', 'exec')`; `from_code` then `exec`s the code object in a fresh namespace pre-seeded with `environment` and `__file__`, which only *defines* functions 
u2014 no template expression runs yet.
`_from_namespace` lifts `name`, `blocks`, `root` and `debug_info` out of the namespace and plants a `__jinja_template__` back-reference in it.
Nothing here sandboxes the generated code. Sandboxing is a different `Environment` subclass that changes *code generation* (`environment.sandboxed`), so it must be chosen before anything is compiled.

open_questions.question: `block_title` and `block_content` are just two functions in a generated module. How does the *parent* template end up calling the child's versions?

answers.answer: In the per-block functions: everything the child actually renders lives inside `block_title` and `block_content`, which are exported through the module-level `blocks` dict.

The compiled Template is cached under (weakref(loader), name); a second lookup returns it after `is_up_to_date` consults DictLoader's uptodate closure, which compares the original source against the current mapping 
u2014 so an edited mapping forces a recompile, but only because `auto_reload` is on.
No. Lexing, parsing and code generation never run template code; the only execution is the `exec` of the generated module, and it merely defines `root` and the block functions.

chapters.title: Handing Over The Data
facts: Caller variables are merged with the globals into `Context.parent`; `Context.vars` starts empty and is reserved for assignments made by generated code.

`Context.__init__` builds a *second* `EvalContext`, so the autoescape callable is consulted again 
u2014 this time at render time, returning True for 'members.html'.
`environment.is_async` is False, so the synchronous path is taken; `render_async` on this template would raise `RuntimeError('The environment was not created with async mode enabled.')`.

`render` wraps the entire render in `except Exception: self.environment.handle_exception()`, which re-raises with a template-aware traceback; `generate()` instead *yields* the handled exception into the stream.

open_questions.question: Escaping was already decided and baked in at compile time, and now a second EvalContext has answered the same question. If the two ever disagreed, which one governs the output?

chapters.title: Fetching The Parent, Then Escaping The Ampersand
chapters.data_out: ' … ' u2014 with `Tom & Jerry` in it
inputs: the constant 'base.html' from the child template's extends
the users list, now inside the Context
facts: Template inheritance is resolved at *render* time, not compile time: the first line of the child's root function performs a live `get_template` call.

`parent` is now 'members.html', so `join_path` runs; the default implementation returns the name unchanged 
u2014 it is the documented hook for making names relative to the importing template.
The parent travels the identical load \u2192 lex \u2192 parse \u2192 generate \u2192 exec path and lands in the same LRUCache, so inheritance costs one extra compile per process, not per render.

Which file an `{% extends %}` / `{% include %}` may reach is delegated entirely to the loader. A template-controlled name is exactly as safe as the loader allows: DictLoader is a key lookup, FileSystemLoader applies `split_template_path` and rejects `..`.

The generated code then runs `for name, parent_block in parent_template.blocks.items(): context.blocks.setdefault(name, []).append(parent_block)` 
u2014 the child's implementation is already at index 0 and the parent's is appended behind it; that ordering is precisely what `super()` walks.

`resolve_or_missing` checks `vars` then `parent`; a name found in neither becomes `environment.undefined(name=...)`, and the default `Undefined` renders as an empty string instead of failing 
u2014 `StrictUndefined` is the opt-in that turns that into an `UndefinedError`.
`user.url` compiles to `environment.getattr(user, 'url')`, which tries the attribute first and then item access, so dict keys are reachable with dot syntax; both failing yields an `Undefined`.

Each interpolated value is wrapped in the `escape(...)` chosen during code generation 
u2014 that is why `'Tom & Jerry'` arrives in the output as `Tom & Jerry`.

The loop compiled to a plain Python `for` over the resolved list with no `LoopContext`, because `find_undeclared` found no use of `loop` in the body 
u2014 the extended loop object is only built when something needs it.
The six `Environment.getattr` calls are the whole dynamic surface of this render: two attribute lookups per user, nothing else reaches outside the context.
The final string is `environment.concat` (`''.join`) over the whole generator, and the child's top-level newlines are absent, exactly as the compiler decided in chapter 5.

answers.answer:
Nothing in the compiler changes 
u2014 `visit_Extends` emits a runtime `environment.get_template(<expr>, 'members.html')`, so a variable target is resolved at render time and the loader is the only thing standing between user data and which template gets loaded.

At render time the child's `context.blocks` already holds its own functions; the extends code appends the parent's blocks behind them, and the parent's root function calls `context.blocks['title'][0](context)` 
u2014 index 0, the child's.

The compile-time decision governs the output: `escape(...)` is literally written into the cached module. The runtime EvalContext only matters for things left volatile (Markup joins, macro autoescape defaults, `context.eval_ctx.autoescape` checks). A callable that changes its answer later will not re-trigger compilation, because the compiled template is cached.
